chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Deals Get Done in India

lessons.title: Open Offers and the SEBI Takeover Code: The 25 Percent Trigger

children.text: In September 2022, the Adani Group completed its purchase of Holcim's controlling stakes in Ambuja Cements and ACC. Holcim, the promoter, got a negotiated exit. But the thousands of retail investors and mutual funds holding Ambuja and ACC had not agreed to anything, and overnight they had a new controlling shareholder they had never chosen. SEBI's answer to that problem is the open offer: when control of a listed company changes hands, public shareholders must also get a chance to sell. Understanding when that right kicks in, and at what price, lets you decide calmly instead of reacting to headlines.

body.text: An open offer is an exit option, not an obligation. SEBI guarantees you the chance to sell when someone takes control, at a price no lower than a formula sets. Whether you should take it depends entirely on how that price compares with the market price and with your view of the new owner.

markDefs.definition: The SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011, which govern disclosures of large shareholdings and open offers when stakes or control of listed companies change.

Persons who cooperate with a common objective of acquiring shares, voting rights or control of a company. Their holdings are added together when testing the thresholds, so splitting a stake among friends does not avoid the rules.

body.caption: When an open offer becomes mandatory

cells: Acquiring shares or voting rights that take the holding to 25% or more
Already holding 25% or more, but below 75%, and acquiring more than 5% in a single financial year
A holding going from 40% to 46% between April and March
Gaining control of the company, such as the right to appoint a majority of directors, at any shareholding level
An investor with 18% signing an agreement giving it the right to appoint most of the board

body.text: Indirect acquisitions count too. Adani did not buy Ambuja and ACC shares from the market. It bought Holcim's holding companies that owned those stakes. Because control of the listed companies changed, open offers were still required. Watch for deals where a company's parent or promoter entity changes hands, because the listed company is swept in.

body.title: Which one triggers an open offer?
body.question: Four fictional investors each change their position in a listed company during the same financial year. Which one must make an open offer?
options: Investor B, already a promoter with 30%, goes to 34%
Investor C, already holding 60%, goes to 64.5%
Investor D holds 18% and signs an agreement giving it the right to appoint a majority of the board
body.explanation: A stays below 25%. B and C already hold more than 25% and add less than 5% in the year (4% and 4.5%), so the creeping acquisition limit is not breached. D is the only trigger: acquiring control requires an open offer regardless of shareholding. Had B gone from 30% to 35.1%, that would also have triggered one.

children.text: How Much the Acquirer Must Offer to Buy

A mandatory open offer must be for at least 26% of the company's total shares. That number is not random: 25% plus 26% takes a fully successful acquirer to at least 51%, a clear majority. The acquirer can offer to buy more, but not less. If shareholders tender more shares than the offer size, the acquirer accepts them on a

body.title: How many of your shares get accepted?
body.prompt: A fictional company, Shivalik Pharma, has 5 crore shares. An acquirer makes an open offer for 26%, or 1.3 crore shares. Shareholders tender 2.6 crore shares in total. Ramesh tendered 400 shares. How many will be accepted?
body.explanation: Acceptance ratio = 1.3 crore ÷ 2.6 crore = 50%. Ramesh's accepted shares = 400 × 50% = 200. The other 200 shares go back to his demat account, and he still holds them at whatever the market price is after the offer.

children.text: The acquirer cannot simply pick a low price. Under Regulation 8, for a company whose shares are frequently traded, the offer price must be at least the highest of four numbers.

body.latex: \text{Minimum offer price} = \max(P_{\text{negotiated}},\; P_{\text{52-wk VWAP paid}},\; P_{\text{26-wk high paid}},\; P_{\text{60-day market VWAP}})
body.caption: The highest negotiated price in the deal that triggered the offer; the volume-weighted average price the acquirer paid in the previous 52 weeks; the highest price it paid in the previous 26 weeks; and the volume-weighted average market price over the 60 trading days before the announcement.

body.title: Shivalik Pharma: the four price tests
Set the minimum offer price
body.prompt: Using the four Shivalik Pharma figures in the chart above, what is the lowest price, in rupees, at which the acquirer can make its open offer?
body.explanation: The minimum offer price is the highest of ₹450, ₹410, ₹465 and ₹438, which is ₹465, the highest price the acquirer paid in the preceding 26 weeks. This stops an acquirer from paying the promoter or itself a high price and offering public shareholders less.

body.text: The formula sets a floor, not a fair price. It looks backwards at prices before the announcement. If the stock rallies after the deal is announced, as it often does, the offer price can end up well below the market price by the time the tendering window opens.

body.label: Adani's 2022 open offers for Ambuja Cements and ACC
body.value: ₹385 per Ambuja share and ₹2,300 per ACC share, each for 26%
body.context: When the tendering window opened, both stocks were trading above their offer prices, so few shareholders tendered. Selling in the market paid more than tendering.

body.title: Remember the size
body.textWithBlank: A mandatory open offer under the Takeover Code must be for at least ___ percent of the company's total shares.
body.explanation: The minimum size is 26%. Combined with the 25% that triggers the offer, a fully subscribed offer takes the acquirer past 51%.

events.title: Public announcement
events.description: Issued through the manager to the offer on the day the acquirer agrees to buy the triggering stake. The stock exchanges disseminate it immediately.

events.title: Detailed public statement
events.description: Published in newspapers, setting out the acquirer, offer price, offer size, reasons and funding. The acquirer must also have deposited money in an escrow account.

events.title: SEBI reviews the draft letter of offer
events.description: SEBI can seek changes. The target's independent directors publish their recommendation on whether the offer is fair.

events.title: Tendering period
events.description: Shareholders tender through the stock exchange mechanism via their broker, for example through the corporate actions section of Zerodha Console.

events.title: Payment
events.description: Accepted shareholders are paid. Unaccepted shares are returned to their demat accounts.

body.title: Can an acquirer walk away once an open offer is announced?

children.text: Only in narrow cases. The Takeover Code allows withdrawal if a required statutory approval is refused, if the acquirer is an individual who dies, or if a condition in the underlying agreement fails for reasons outside the acquirer's control and that condition was disclosed upfront. An acquirer cannot withdraw because the share price fell or it changed its mind. The escrow deposit exists precisely so that SEBI can enforce payment.

Separately, anyone can make a voluntary open offer, and a rival bidder can make a competing offer. Hostile takeovers remain rare in India because promoters usually hold large stakes, but L&T's 2019 acquisition of Mindtree against the wishes of its founders showed that they are possible.

body.title: Reasons to tender vs reasons to hold

columns.label: Lean towards tendering
points: Offer price is clearly above the market price during the tendering period
You do not trust the new controlling shareholder
You expect the share price to fall back once the offer closes
You wanted to exit anyway and the offer gives a better price
Remember that only part of your tender may be accepted

columns.label: Lean towards holding or selling in the market
points: Market price is at or above the offer price, so selling on NSE or BSE pays more or the same
The new owner brings capital, scale or better management you want exposure to
You believe the business is worth more than the offer price over time
Tax is rarely a deciding factor, since shares tendered through the exchange are taxed much like a market sale
Your shares stay liquid, while tendered shares are blocked until the offer is settled

body.title: The Shivalik Pharma decision
body.scenario: Shivalik Pharma's open offer is at ₹465 for 26% of the company. When the tendering window opens, the stock trades at ₹448. You hold 1,000 shares bought at ₹300. Market chatter suggests heavy tendering, and the acquirer is a large, well-run pharma group that plans to use Shivalik as its India manufacturing base.
body.prompt: Should you tender, hold or sell in the market? Work through the numbers and the risks.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Premium: ₹465 minus ₹448 = ₹17 per share, about 3.8% over the market price.
2. Pro-rata risk: if tendering is heavy, as in the earlier example where 2.6 crore shares chased 1.3 crore, maybe only half your 1,000 shares get accepted. That is 500 × ₹17 = ₹8,500 extra, not ₹17,000.
3. What happens to the rest: after the offer closes, the price often drifts back towards where it would trade without the offer. If it falls to, say, ₹430, the loss on your unaccepted 500 shares (500 × ₹18 = ₹9,000) could wipe out the gain.
4. The new owner: a strong acquirer planning to invest in Shivalik is a reason some shareholders prefer to stay invested for the long term.
5. A reasonable approach: if you want to stay invested, hold. If you want out, tender everything, because tendering carries no cost, and then sell any returned shares in the market. Do not decide based only on the ₹17 headline premium.
6. Tax: tendered shares sold through the exchange are taxed like a market sale. Lesson 5.1 covers the details.

body.title: When a stock you own announces an open offer
steps: Confirm the trigger and who the acquirer is from the public announcement on BSE or NSE
Note the offer price, offer size and tendering dates from the detailed public statement
Read the independent directors' recommendation on the offer price
Compare the offer price with the market price just before tendering opens
Estimate how many of your shares might be accepted if the offer is oversubscribed
Decide whether you want exposure to the company under its new owner

body.label: SEBI: Takeover Open Offers
body.description: SEBI's website lists draft and final letters of offer under its filings section, with offer prices, sizes and timelines for every open offer.

cards.definition: The SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011.
Acquiring 25% or more of the shares or voting rights of a listed company requires an open offer.
A holder between 25% and 75% acquiring more than 5% in a financial year, which triggers an open offer.
Acquiring control of a listed company requires an open offer at any shareholding level.
26% of the company's total shares for a mandatory open offer.
The highest of the negotiated price, the acquirer's 52-week VWAP paid, its highest price paid in 26 weeks and the 60-day market VWAP.
When an offer is oversubscribed, each shareholder's tender is accepted in the same ratio.
Parties cooperating to acquire shares or control, whose holdings are combined for the thresholds.

points: An open offer is triggered by crossing 25%, by a holder between 25% and 75% adding more than 5% in a financial year, or by acquiring control at any level.
Indirect acquisitions count: Adani's purchase of Holcim's holding entities required open offers for both Ambuja Cements and ACC.
A mandatory offer must be for at least 26% of total shares, and oversubscribed offers are accepted proportionately.
The offer price must be at least the highest of four backward-looking prices, which is a floor, not a guarantee of a good price.
Tender only after comparing the offer price with the live market price and estimating how many shares will actually be accepted.
Tendering is optional. Holding means staying invested under the new controlling shareholder.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Shivalik Pharma and the investors in the examples are fictional. The regulatory thresholds and timelines are simplified summaries of the SEBI Takeover Regulations, 2011 as generally applied, and individual offers can involve additional conditions. Figures for real companies are taken from public disclosures. Always read the letter of offer before tendering.
